plans.title: Getting to Know Jesus
plans.subtitle: A 7-Day Bible Reading Plan for New Believers
purpose: Following Jesus begins with knowing who He is, why He came, and what it means to trust Him. Over the next seven days, you will read key passages from the Bible that introduce Jesus as the Son of God, Savior, Teacher, Shepherd, risen Lord, and faithful Friend. Each day includes a short explanation, a question for reflection, a prayer prompt, and a practical step.

Read each passage slowly. Ask God to help you understand His Word, and write down anything that teaches you about the character, words, or work of Jesus. You do not need to understand everything at once. The goal is to take one faithful step each day as you grow in your relationship with Him.

closing.heading: Continue the Journey
paragraphs: These seven days are only a beginning. Continue getting to know Jesus by reading the Gospel of John, speaking with Him in prayer, connecting with a Bible-believing church, and learning alongside mature Christians. When questions arise, bring them honestly to God and return to His Word. Jesus invites you not merely to know facts about Him, but to trust Him, walk with Him, and grow in His grace. If you are still exploring who Jesus is, continue seeking Him through Scripture. Consider what you have learned about His identity, His sacrifice, and His resurrection. Jesus calls you to turn from sin and trust Him as Savior and Lord. Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ, not something you can earn through good works. If you have already placed your faith in Christ, continue growing in your relationship with Him through Scripture, prayer, obedience, and fellowship with other believers.

lessons.title: Jesus Is the Son of God

keyVerse.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

lessons.devotionalThought: John introduces Jesus as “the Word,” who existed with God and is God. Jesus did not begin at Bethlehem; He is eternal. Yet He willingly entered our world and became fully human without ceasing to be fully God. Through Jesus, we see God’s glory, grace, and truth. Getting to know Jesus therefore means more than learning about a historical teacher. It means meeting the eternal Son of God who came near so that we could know the Father.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What does this passage teach you about who Jesus is?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, help me see You as You truly are and grow in my understanding of Your grace and truth.
lessons.practicalStep: Write down three descriptions of Jesus found in John 1:1–18.

lessons.title: Jesus Came to Save Sinners

keyVerse.text: For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.

lessons.devotionalThought: Zacchaeus was rejected by many people because of his dishonest lifestyle, but Jesus saw him, called him by name, and entered his home. Jesus did not approve of Zacchaeus’s sin; His grace led Zacchaeus to genuine repentance and a changed life. This is good news for every new believer: Jesus seeks people who are spiritually lost and offers salvation to those who trust Him. No past failure places a repentant person beyond His mercy. Zacchaeus did not earn Jesus' acceptance by changing his behavior; his changed behavior demonstrated the transformation taking place in his heart.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How did meeting Jesus change Zacchaeus’s attitudes and actions?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, thank You for seeking me and offering forgiveness. Show me any area of my life that needs to change.
lessons.practicalStep: Confess one known sin to God and identify one step of repentance you can take today.

lessons.title: Jesus Teaches the Way of Life

keyVerse.text: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.

lessons.devotionalThought: Jesus teaches that life in God’s kingdom begins in the heart. He calls blessed those who recognize their spiritual need, mourn over sin, seek righteousness, show mercy, pursue purity, and make peace. His followers are also called to be salt and light in the world. Good works do not earn salvation; they are the visible fruit of a life being changed by God and should direct attention to Him.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which quality in the Beatitudes do you most need Jesus to develop in you?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, shape my character so that my life reflects Your goodness and points others to the Father.
lessons.practicalStep: Choose one quiet act of mercy, encouragement, or service to complete today.

lessons.title: Jesus Is the Good Shepherd

keyVerse.text: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.

lessons.devotionalThought: Jesus describes Himself as the Good Shepherd who knows, leads, protects, and lays down His life for His sheep. Unlike a hired worker who runs when danger comes, Jesus remains faithful. His care is personal: He knows those who belong to Him, and they learn to recognize His voice. New believers grow in this relationship by listening to His Word, trusting His direction, and following Him one step at a time.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What does the picture of Jesus as your Shepherd reveal about His care for you?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, teach me to recognize Your voice in Scripture and to follow You with trust.
lessons.practicalStep: Note one instruction from today’s passage that you can obey this week.

lessons.title: Jesus Gave His Life for Us

keyVerse.text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

lessons.devotionalThought: The cross was not an accident or a defeat. Long before Jesus was crucified, Isaiah described the suffering Servant who would bear the sins of others. On the cross, Jesus willingly took the judgment sinners deserve so that those who trust Him could be forgiven and reconciled to God. His sacrifice reveals both the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God’s love. Salvation rests in what Christ has done, not in our ability to make ourselves worthy. The healing Isaiah describes is rooted in Christ's saving work, through which sinners can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What does the cross teach you about your sin and Jesus’ love?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, thank You for bearing my sin and giving Your life for me. Help me rest in Your finished work.
lessons.practicalStep: Write a brief thank-you prayer focused only on what Jesus accomplished on the cross.

lessons.title: Jesus Is Risen

keyVerse.text: He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee,

lessons.devotionalThought: Jesus truly died, was buried, and rose bodily from the grave. The empty tomb and the witnesses who saw the risen Christ stand at the center of the Christian faith. His resurrection confirms who He is, shows that His sacrifice was accepted, and gives believers the sure hope of eternal life. Christians do not merely follow the teachings of someone who died; they worship and follow a living Savior.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Why is the resurrection essential to your faith and hope?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Risen Jesus, strengthen my faith and help me live with the hope and confidence of Your victory.
lessons.practicalStep: Tell someone you trust one reason the resurrection gives you hope.

lessons.title: Jesus Calls Us to Follow Him

keyVerse.text: And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.

lessons.devotionalThought: Knowing Jesus leads to following Jesus. He calls believers to surrender self-rule, remain close to Him, obey His words, and depend on Him for spiritual fruit. This does not mean earning His love through perfect performance. It means responding to His grace with faithful trust and obedience. As a branch receives life from the vine, you will grow by abiding in Christ through Scripture, prayer, fellowship, and daily dependence on Him.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What is one area of your life that Jesus is asking you to surrender to His leadership?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, I choose to follow You. Help me remain close to You and obey You each day.
lessons.practicalStep: Choose a regular time and place for Bible reading and prayer during the coming week.

plans.title: Finding Hope in Scripture
plans.subtitle: A 7-Day Bible Reading Plan for New Believers
purpose: Hope is more than wishing that life will improve. Biblical hope is a confident trust in God—His character, His promises, and His saving work through Jesus Christ. During the next seven days, you will read passages that show where lasting hope is found and how God’s truth steadies believers during uncertainty, sorrow, waiting, and fear.

Begin each day by asking God to help you understand and believe His Word. Read the entire passage slowly, paying attention to what it reveals about God and His promises. You may still experience difficult emotions, but you can learn to bring them honestly to the Lord and anchor your heart in what He has said.

closing.heading: Continue in Hope
paragraphs: Hope grows as you return to God’s truth again and again. Continue reading Scripture, bring your concerns to God in prayer, and stay connected to a Bible-believing church and mature Christians who can encourage you. Consider reading the Gospel of John, Psalms 23, 27, 46, and 121, and Romans 5–8 next. When discouragement returns, remember that your hope is not built on changing circumstances but on the unchanging character of God and the finished work of Jesus Christ.

lessons.title: Hope Begins with God

keyVerse.text: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.

lessons.devotionalThought: The psalmist does not pretend that everything is easy. He speaks honestly about his sadness, spiritual thirst, and unanswered questions. Yet he also speaks truth to his own soul: “hope thou in God.” Biblical hope does not deny pain; it directs us to the One who remains faithful in the middle of it. When your feelings are unsettled, you can remember who God is and choose to trust that He is still present and worthy of praise.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What burden do you need to bring honestly before God today?
lessons.prayerPrompt: God, when my heart is discouraged, help me place my hope in You and remember Your faithful presence.
lessons.practicalStep: Write down one discouraging thought, then answer it with one truth about God from Psalm 42.

lessons.title: Hope in God’s Unchanging Word

keyVerse.text: Thou art my hiding place and my shield: I hope in thy word.

lessons.devotionalThought: God’s Word gives light when the path ahead is unclear. The writer of Psalm 119 faced trouble, but he found security in what God had spoken. Circumstances and emotions can change quickly; God’s truth does not. Scripture teaches us who God is, corrects our thinking, and gives us promises to remember. Hope grows as we learn God’s Word and rely on it rather than allowing fear to have the final word.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Where do you most need the guidance of God’s Word right now?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Lord, make Your Word a light for my path and teach me to trust what You have spoken.
lessons.practicalStep: Copy Psalm 119:114 somewhere you will see it throughout the day.

lessons.title: Hope When You Are Afraid

keyVerse.text: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.

lessons.devotionalThought: God spoke these words to Israel, His chosen people, reminding them of His covenant faithfulness. He did not simply command them not to fear; He gave them reasons for courage. He promised His presence, strength, help, and sustaining care. Christians today can draw encouragement from the same unchanging character of God, knowing through Jesus Christ that He remains faithful to those who belong to Him. Hope is not confidence in our own ability to control every outcome. It is confidence that the Lord will not abandon His people. When fear rises, you can turn your attention from the size of the problem to the faithfulness and power of God.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which promise in Isaiah 41:10 speaks most directly to your present fear?
lessons.prayerPrompt: God, help me trust Your presence and strength when I feel afraid or uncertain.
lessons.practicalStep: Name one fear in prayer and repeat the promises of Isaiah 41:10 after you name it.

lessons.title: Hope in God’s Mercy

keyVerse.text: It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.

lessons.devotionalThought: These words were written during a season of deep grief and devastation. In the middle of sorrow, the writer deliberately remembers God’s mercy, compassion, and faithfulness. The Lord’s goodness had not disappeared simply because life was painful. Even amid devastating circumstances, God's compassion had not been exhausted. His faithfulness remained the foundation of hope for those who continued to seek Him. When yesterday has been difficult, God’s mercy gives you a reason to seek Him again today.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How have you seen God’s mercy or provision, even during a difficult season?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Faithful Lord, thank You that Your compassion does not fail. Help me wait for You with hope.
lessons.practicalStep: List three mercies from God that you can recognize today.

lessons.title: Hope Through Jesus Christ

keyVerse.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,

lessons.devotionalThought: Christian hope is alive because Jesus is alive. Through Christ’s death and resurrection, believers receive new life and an eternal inheritance that cannot be destroyed. Trials may test faith, but they cannot undo what God has secured in Christ. Your hope rests not in avoiding every hardship but in belonging to the risen Savior, who is keeping you and preparing an everlasting future with Him.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How does the resurrection of Jesus give you hope beyond your present circumstances?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, thank You for giving me living hope through Your resurrection. Help me trust what You have secured for me.
lessons.practicalStep: Share with someone one reason your hope in Christ is different from ordinary optimism.

lessons.title: Hope While You Wait

keyVerse.text: But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it.

lessons.devotionalThought: Waiting can be difficult because we cannot yet see the outcome. Romans 8 reminds us that creation groans, believers experience weakness, and we do not always know what to pray. Yet the Holy Spirit helps us, and God continues working according to His wise purpose. Hope enables patient endurance—not because we understand every detail, but because the God who saves us is at work even when His work is not yet visible.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What are you waiting for, and how might God be teaching you to trust Him during the wait?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, give me patience when I cannot see the outcome, and help me trust that You are still at work.
lessons.practicalStep: Turn one area of waiting into a written prayer of surrender and trust.

lessons.title: Hope for the Future

keyVerse.text: And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

lessons.devotionalThought: Scripture ends by directing believers toward the future God has promised. Sin, death, sorrow, and pain will not last forever. God will dwell with His people, make all things new, and fully remove every effect of the fall. This is God's promise of what is to come, not a guarantee that believers will be spared grief, sickness, or hardship in this present life. This promise does not make present suffering unimportant; it assures us that suffering will not have the final word. Because God is faithful, believers can endure today while looking forward to eternity with Him.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which part of God’s promised future gives you the greatest encouragement?
lessons.prayerPrompt: God, keep my heart fixed on Your promise to make all things new, and help me live faithfully while I wait.
lessons.practicalStep: Write one sentence describing how eternal hope can change the way you face today.

plans.title: Learning to Trust God
plans.subtitle: A 7-Day Bible Reading Plan for New Believers
purpose: Trusting God means relying on His character, wisdom, and promises even when you cannot see the entire path ahead. During the next seven days, you will read passages that explain why God is trustworthy and how faith grows through knowing His Word, surrendering your fears, obeying His direction, and remembering His faithfulness.

Begin each day with a simple prayer asking God to teach you. Read the entire passage slowly, notice what it reveals about God, and honestly bring Him your questions. Trust often grows one decision at a time. You do not need to have every answer; you can learn to depend on the One who does.

closing.heading: Continue Learning to Trust
paragraphs: Trust grows through an ongoing relationship with God. Continue reading His Word, speaking honestly with Him in prayer, obeying what He teaches, and remembering how He has been faithful. Stay connected to a Bible-believing church and mature Christians who can encourage you. When doubts or fears return, do not hide them from God. Bring them to Him and choose again to rely on His character, promises, and saving love in Jesus Christ.

lessons.title: Trust God with Your Whole Heart

keyVerse.text: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.

lessons.devotionalThought: Trusting God begins with recognizing that His wisdom is greater than ours. Our understanding is limited, and circumstances can confuse us, but God sees the whole picture. This passage does not tell us to stop thinking; it warns us not to make our own judgment the final authority. As we acknowledge God in every part of life, we can trust His wisdom to guide us. This does not mean He will reveal every detail of the road ahead, but that we should seek His direction through Scripture, prayer, and wise counsel while walking faithfully in what He has made clear.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: In what area are you relying most heavily on your own understanding?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Lord, help me trust You with my whole heart and submit my plans to Your wisdom.
lessons.practicalStep: Write down one decision you are facing and ask God to direct you through His Word and wise counsel.

lessons.title: Trust God Because He Is Faithful

keyVerse.text: Know therefore that the LORD thy God, he is God, the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations;

lessons.devotionalThought: Moses reminded Israel that the Lord had chosen them and remained faithful to His covenant promises. This passage reveals something essential about God's character: He is faithful, unchanging, and true to His Word. Christians can trust that same faithful God, whose saving promises are fulfilled through Jesus Christ. People may disappoint us, and our own resolve may weaken, but God remains true to His character and His Word. Learning His past acts of faithfulness gives us strong reasons to trust Him today.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What does God’s faithfulness mean for the concern you are carrying today?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Faithful God, help me remember that You always remain true to Your character and promises.
lessons.practicalStep: Record one example of God’s faithfulness from Scripture and one from your own life.

lessons.title: Trust God with Your Fears

keyVerse.text: What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.

lessons.devotionalThought: David does not say that trusting God means never feeling afraid. He acknowledges his fear and then deliberately turns toward God. Fear may alert us to uncertainty, but it does not have to control our response. We can pray honestly, remember God’s Word, and choose to place our confidence in Him. Trust is often the faithful decision we make while fear is still present.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What fear do you need to place into God’s hands?
lessons.prayerPrompt: God, when I am afraid, help me turn to You, remember Your Word, and trust Your care.
lessons.practicalStep: Name your fear in writing, then write Psalm 56:3 beneath it as your response of faith.

lessons.title: Trust God in the Waiting

keyVerse.text: Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD.

lessons.devotionalThought: Waiting can expose how strongly we want immediate answers and control. David faced enemies and uncertainty, yet he sought the Lord and expected to see His goodness. Waiting on God is not passive resignation. It is active dependence—continuing to pray, obey, and hope while trusting God’s timing. The Lord can strengthen your heart before He changes your circumstances.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What makes waiting difficult for you in your present situation?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Lord, give me courage and strengthen my heart as I wait for Your timing.
lessons.practicalStep: Choose one faithful action you can take today without trying to force the outcome.

lessons.title: Trust God Enough to Obey

keyVerse.text: So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him; and Lot went with him: and Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran.

lessons.devotionalThought: God called Abram to leave what was familiar and go to a land that He would show him. Abram did not receive every detail beforehand, but he responded to God’s word with obedience. Trust becomes visible when we act on what God has clearly said. We are saved by grace, not by our works, yet genuine faith learns to follow God even when the next step feels uncertain.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Is there a clear biblical instruction you know but have hesitated to obey?
lessons.prayerPrompt: God, give me faith to obey what You have shown me, even when I cannot see every step ahead.
lessons.practicalStep: Identify one clear act of obedience and take the first step today.

lessons.title: Trust God in Every Need

keyVerse.text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.

lessons.devotionalThought: Jesus teaches that our heavenly Father knows what we need. Worry cannot secure tomorrow, but it can distract us from faithful obedience today. Jesus points to God’s care in creation and calls His followers to seek God’s kingdom first. This does not mean ignoring responsibilities. It means carrying them with confidence that the Father sees, knows, and cares for His children. Trusting God's provision does not mean that believers will never experience hardship, financial difficulty, or unmet expectations. It means seeking His kingdom first and relying on His faithful care, even when circumstances are difficult.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which need or concern most often draws your attention away from God?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, help me seek Your kingdom first and trust You with my daily needs.
lessons.practicalStep: When worry returns today, pause to pray and complete the next responsible task in front of you.

lessons.title: Trust God with Your Future

keyVerse.text: He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?

lessons.devotionalThought: The cross is the clearest evidence that God is committed to the good of His people. He did not spare His own Son but gave Him for our salvation. Believers may face hardship, uncertainty, or loss, but none of these can separate them from the love of God in Christ. We may not know every detail of the future, yet we can entrust ourselves to the God who has already demonstrated His love and who works according to His wise purpose. God's promise to work all things together for good does not mean that every circumstance will turn out as we desire. In the context of Romans 8, His ultimate purpose is to conform believers to the image of His Son and bring them to final glory.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How does the gift of Jesus strengthen your confidence in God’s care for your future?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, thank You for proving Your love through Jesus. Help me entrust my future to You.
lessons.practicalStep: Write a short statement of trust that begins, “Because God gave His Son for me, I can trust Him with…”

plans.title: Beginning Your Walk with Christ
plans.subtitle: A 7-Day Bible Reading Plan for New Believers
purpose: Beginning your walk with Christ is the start of a lifelong relationship with Him. During the next seven days, you will explore essential truths that help new believers understand salvation, their new identity, prayer, Scripture, obedience, Christian fellowship, and daily dependence on Jesus.

Begin each day by asking God to help you understand His Word. Read the entire passage slowly, reflect honestly, and complete the practical step. Spiritual growth does not happen through perfection or self-effort. It develops as you trust Christ, depend on the Holy Spirit, and respond faithfully to what God teaches you.

closing.heading: Continue Your Walk
paragraphs: Your first steps with Christ are the beginning of lifelong growth. Continue reading the Bible, praying honestly, obeying what God teaches, and participating in a faithful local church. When you sin, confess it and return to the grace of Christ. When you have questions, seek answers in Scripture and learn from mature believers. Keep your attention fixed on Jesus, trusting that He who saved you will continue His work in you.

lessons.title: Receive New Life in Christ

keyVerse.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

lessons.devotionalThought: Christianity begins not with trying harder but with receiving new life from God. Jesus told Nicodemus that a person must be born again. This new birth is the work of the Holy Spirit, who gives spiritual life to those who belong to Christ. Salvation is not something we produce through our own efforts; it is God's gracious work, received through faith in Jesus Christ. We cannot save ourselves through morality, religion, or good works. God lovingly gave His Son so that everyone who believes in Him may receive everlasting life. Your walk with Christ begins by trusting who Jesus is and what He has done for you.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What does this passage teach you about how a person receives eternal life?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, thank You for giving Yourself for me. Help me trust You fully and rest in the salvation You provide.
lessons.practicalStep: Write a brief statement explaining what you believe about Jesus and why you are trusting Him.

lessons.title: Understand Your New Identity

keyVerse.text: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.

lessons.devotionalThought: When you trust Christ, God gives you a new identity. Your past no longer has the final word over who you are. You are reconciled to God, brought into a new relationship with Him, and called to represent Christ to others. Becoming a new creation in Christ does not mean you will never struggle with sin or immediately overcome every old habit. It means God has given you a new identity and a new direction for your life. Spiritual growth takes time as you learn to depend on His grace, obey His Word, and follow the leading of the Holy Spirit.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How does being “in Christ” change the way you view yourself and your past?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, help me understand my new identity in Christ and live in the freedom of Your grace.
lessons.practicalStep: Write down one old label you need to release and one biblical truth about who you are in Christ.

lessons.title: Grow Through God’s Word

keyVerse.text: Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.

lessons.devotionalThought: Scripture teaches you what is true, reveals God’s character, corrects wrong thinking, and equips you to live faithfully. Reading the Bible is not merely gathering information; it is learning to know, trust, and obey God. Consistent time in His Word will shape your mind and strengthen your walk with Christ.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What habit could help you engage with Scripture consistently?
lessons.prayerPrompt: God, give me a hunger for Your Word and help me understand, remember, and obey it.
lessons.practicalStep: Choose a regular time and place for Bible reading, and begin with the Gospel of John.

lessons.title: Learn to Pray

keyVerse.text: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.

lessons.devotionalThought: Prayer is honest conversation with your heavenly Father. Jesus teaches His followers to approach God with reverence, seek His will, ask for daily needs, confess sin, extend forgiveness, and request protection from temptation. You do not need impressive words. Because of Christ, you may come to God sincerely and confidently.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which part of the Lord’s Prayer do you most need to include in your prayers?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, teach me to pray with honesty, humility, and confidence in Your care.
lessons.practicalStep: Use Matthew 6:9–13 as an outline for a personal prayer today.

lessons.title: Follow Christ in Obedience

keyVerse.text: If ye love me, keep my commandments.

lessons.devotionalThought: Obedience is not a way to earn salvation; it is a loving response to the Savior who has rescued you. Jesus also promises the Holy Spirit, who teaches and helps believers. As you learn Christ’s commands, ask the Spirit to give you understanding and strength. A growing Christian does not obey perfectly, but increasingly desires to please the Lord and turns back to Him after failure.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What teaching of Jesus do you need to put into practice?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, help me respond to Your love with willing obedience and depend on the Holy Spirit.
lessons.practicalStep: Identify one command from your recent Bible reading and take a specific step to obey it.

lessons.title: Grow with Other Believers

keyVerse.text: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.

lessons.devotionalThought: God did not design Christians to grow alone. The first believers devoted themselves to biblical teaching, fellowship, shared meals, prayer, generosity, and worship. A healthy local church provides opportunities to learn, serve, receive encouragement, and encourage others. Christian community will not be perfect, but it is an important part of God’s plan for your growth. The early believers also responded to the gospel through baptism, publicly identifying themselves with Jesus Christ. Baptism does not earn salvation; it is an important act of obedience and a visible expression of faith in the Savior who has already provided salvation by grace.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Why do you think fellowship with other believers is essential to spiritual growth?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Lord, lead me to a faithful church community where I can learn, worship, serve, and grow.
lessons.practicalStep: If you are not connected to a Bible-believing church, identify one to visit or ask a mature Christian for guidance.

lessons.title: Walk with Christ Every Day

keyVerse.text: As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him:

lessons.devotionalThought: The Christian life continues the same way it begins—by faith in Christ. To walk in Him means depending on Him daily, becoming rooted in His truth, growing in faith, and living with gratitude. Be careful not to let ideas contrary to Scripture draw you away from Christ. Everything you need for spiritual life is found in Him, and He will remain faithful as you continue following Him. There will be seasons of growth, struggle, questions, and even failure along the way. When those times come, return to Christ, confess your sins, and continue walking in His grace. Your relationship with Him rests on His saving work, not on your ability to live a perfect Christian life.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What daily practice will help you remain rooted and growing in Christ?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Jesus, help me walk with You each day, remain grounded in truth, and grow in grateful faith.
lessons.practicalStep: Create a simple weekly rhythm that includes Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship, and service.

plans.title: How to Pray Through Scripture
plans.subtitle: A 7-Day Bible Reading Plan for New Believers
purpose: Praying through Scripture means allowing God’s Word to guide your conversation with Him. Instead of searching for perfect words, you read a passage, notice what it reveals, and respond with worship, confession, thanksgiving, requests, and surrender. During the next seven days, you will practice turning different kinds of biblical passages into personal prayer.

Begin by reading the entire passage slowly. Ask: What does this teach me about God? Is there a truth to praise Him for, a sin to confess, a promise to trust, a command to obey, or a need to bring before Him? Then respond in your own words. Always read verses in their context; praying Scripture is responding faithfully to what God has said, not claiming every biblical statement as an unconditional personal promise.

closing.heading: Continue Praying Through Scripture
paragraphs: Use this simple pattern as you continue: read the passage carefully, understand it in context, notice what it reveals, and respond to God. You may praise Him for His character, confess sin exposed by His Word, thank Him for His works, ask for help, pray for others, and surrender to His will. The Psalms, the prayers of Jesus, and the prayers in Paul’s letters are especially helpful places to practice. Over time, Scripture will enlarge your prayers, correct your priorities, and deepen your relationship with God.

lessons.title: Begin with Praise

keyVerse.text: Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.

lessons.devotionalThought: Scripture gives us true words and worthy reasons for praising God. Psalm 145 celebrates His greatness, goodness, compassion, and mighty works. As you read, pause whenever you see something about God’s character and turn it into praise. This shifts prayer away from being only a list of needs and helps you begin with the One to whom you are praying.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which description of God in this passage most strengthens your worship?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Lord, You are great, gracious, compassionate, and worthy of praise. Help me honor You for who You are.
lessons.practicalStep: Choose three truths about God from Psalm 145:1–9 and speak each one back to Him in praise.

lessons.title: Confess Sin Honestly

keyVerse.text: Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.

lessons.devotionalThought: David’s prayer shows that confession is honest agreement with God about sin. He does not excuse, minimize, or hide what he has done. He appeals to God’s mercy and asks for cleansing, renewal, and restored fellowship. Through Jesus Christ, believers can come directly to God to confess their sins and seek His forgiveness. We do not need to hide our failures or earn our way back into His favor. Christ's sacrifice provides the foundation for forgiveness, and genuine repentance turns us back toward obedience to God.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Is there any attitude, action, or pattern you have been reluctant to confess?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Merciful God, show me my sin, help me confess it without excuse, and cleanse me through Your grace.
lessons.practicalStep: Use Psalm 51:1–12 as a guide to name one sin, ask forgiveness, and request a renewed heart.

lessons.title: Give Thanks for God’s Goodness

keyVerse.text: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:

lessons.devotionalThought: Thanksgiving remembers what God has done. Psalm 103 names His forgiveness, healing, redemption, mercy, compassion, and patient care. God's healing power is worthy of thanksgiving, but this passage should not be understood as a guarantee that every illness will be healed in this life. We can pray confidently for His help while trusting His wisdom and remembering that complete freedom from suffering awaits the restoration He has promised through Christ. When discouragement narrows your attention to what is wrong, Scripture helps you remember God’s benefits without denying present difficulties. Gratitude grows as you connect biblical truth with specific evidence of God’s grace.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which of God’s benefits in this passage are you especially thankful for today?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, keep me from forgetting Your goodness. Thank You for Your mercy, forgiveness, and faithful care.
lessons.practicalStep: Make a list of five gifts from God, connecting each one to a phrase from Psalm 103.

lessons.title: Bring Your Fears to God

keyVerse.text: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?

lessons.devotionalThought: David speaks about danger honestly, but he also declares what is true about God. Praying through fear involves both naming what troubles you and answering it with God’s character. The Lord is light when you cannot see clearly, salvation when you feel threatened, and strength when you feel weak. Scripture teaches you to seek His presence rather than allowing fear to direct your life.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What fear needs to be answered with the truth of who God is?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Lord, You are my light, salvation, and strength. Help me seek You and trust You in what frightens me.
lessons.practicalStep: Write one fear, then turn three truths from Psalm 27 into a prayer of trust.

lessons.title: Pray God’s Promises in Context

keyVerse.text: Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

lessons.devotionalThought: God’s promises give believers firm ground for prayer. Romans 8 does not promise an easy life, but it does promise that God works according to His wise purpose and that nothing can separate His people from His love in Christ. Read the whole paragraph so that your prayer reflects what the promise truly says. Then thank God for it, ask for help believing it, and bring your circumstances under its truth.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which promise in Romans 8:28–39 do you find hardest to believe during difficulty?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, thank You that nothing can separate me from Your love in Christ. Help me trust Your purpose when I do not understand.
lessons.practicalStep: Select one promise from the passage and pray it in three parts: thank God, confess your struggle to believe, and ask for faith.

lessons.title: Pray for Wisdom and Obedience

keyVerse.text: For this cause we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you, and to desire that ye might be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding;

lessons.devotionalThought: Paul’s prayer shows that we may ask God for more than immediate relief. We can pray for spiritual wisdom, a life that pleases the Lord, fruitful obedience, endurance, joy, and gratitude. Apostolic prayers like this one teach us priorities that reflect God’s will. You can pray these requests for yourself and for other believers by carefully placing their needs into the prayer’s biblical pattern.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which spiritual need in Paul’s prayer is most important for you right now?
lessons.prayerPrompt: God, fill me with the knowledge of Your will, strengthen me to obey, and make my life fruitful and thankful.
lessons.practicalStep: Pray Colossians 1:9–14 for yourself, then pray it for one other person by name.

lessons.title: Surrender Your Plans to God

keyVerse.text: Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.

lessons.devotionalThought: Scripture-shaped prayer brings our plans under God’s authority. Jesus teaches us to desire the Father’s kingdom and will, while James warns against planning as though we control tomorrow. Surrender is not refusing to make plans; it is holding them humbly before God and asking Him to redirect us. We learn to want His glory and purposes more than our preferred outcome.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What plan or desired outcome is difficult for you to surrender to God?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, let Your kingdom come and Your will be done in my life. Direct my plans and make me willing to obey.
lessons.practicalStep: Write one plan before God and pray, “If the Lord will,” asking for wisdom, humility, and obedience.

plans.title: Understanding the Holy Spirit
plans.subtitle: A 7-Day Bible Reading Plan for New Believers
purpose: The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force. He is God, the third Person of the Trinity, who gives spiritual life, lives within believers, reveals truth through Scripture, produces Christlike character, helps us pray, and empowers us to follow Jesus. During the next seven days, you will explore who the Holy Spirit is and how believers can depend on His presence and work.

Begin each day by asking God to help you understand His Word. Read the entire passage slowly and in context. Pay attention to what the text teaches about the Holy Spirit rather than relying only on feelings or personal impressions. The goal is not merely to learn facts about Him, but to grow in grateful, obedient dependence on God.

closing.heading: Continue Walking by the Spirit
paragraphs: Continue learning about the Holy Spirit by reading Romans 8, John 14–16, 1 Corinthians 12, Galatians 5, and Ephesians 4–6. Dependence on the Spirit grows as you remain in Scripture, pray, turn from sin, participate in a faithful local church, and obey what God makes clear. Avoid judging His work only by dramatic experiences. Look also for His steady work of glorifying Christ, illuminating truth, producing holiness, strengthening prayer, and equipping believers to serve others.

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit Is God

keyVerse.text: Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.

lessons.devotionalThought: Scripture presents the Holy Spirit as a divine Person, not merely a power or influence. Peter explains that lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God, and Jesus names the Holy Ghost together with the Father and the Son. The Spirit speaks, teaches, guides, can be grieved, and acts according to His will. Knowing this helps new believers approach Him with reverence and trust.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How does recognizing the Holy Spirit as God change the way you think about His presence?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Holy Spirit, help me know You according to Scripture and honor You as God.
lessons.practicalStep: Write down three truths from today’s passages that show the Holy Spirit is personal and divine.

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit Gives New Life

keyVerse.text: That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.

lessons.devotionalThought: Jesus teaches that entering God’s kingdom requires new birth by the Holy Spirit. Salvation is not achieved through human effort or religious improvement. The Spirit gives spiritual life, applies God’s saving work to us, and begins the renewal that continues throughout the Christian life. Every believer therefore depends on the Spirit from the very beginning. This new life is made possible through Jesus Christ and His saving work. We do not earn salvation through religious effort or good behavior; we receive God's gift of salvation through faith in Christ, and the Holy Spirit brings spiritual renewal into our lives.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What do these passages teach you about the difference between self-improvement and spiritual rebirth?
lessons.prayerPrompt: God, thank You for giving new life through the Holy Spirit. Continue renewing me by Your grace.
lessons.practicalStep: Write a short prayer thanking God that salvation and renewal are His work rather than something you must earn.

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit Lives in Believers

keyVerse.text: The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:

lessons.devotionalThought: Everyone who belongs to Christ has the Holy Spirit. His indwelling presence marks believers as God’s people and assures them that they are His children. The Spirit does not make Christians independent of God; He draws them into deeper dependence, teaching them to approach the Father and live according to their new identity rather than returning to the rule of sin.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What encouragement do you receive from knowing that the Holy Spirit lives within every believer?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Father, thank You for giving me Your Spirit and bringing me into Your family through Christ.
lessons.practicalStep: List two truths from Romans 8:9–17 about what the Spirit’s presence means for a believer.

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit Teaches Through Scripture

keyVerse.text: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.

lessons.devotionalThought: Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit would teach the apostles and bring His words to their remembrance. The Spirit guided them into truth and glorified Christ, providing the foundation for the New Testament witness. Today, He helps believers understand and apply the Scripture He inspired. His guidance will never contradict God’s written Word or draw attention away from Jesus. The Holy Spirit's work of illuminating Scripture helps us understand and apply God's revealed truth; it does not give us authority to add new teachings to Scripture or treat personal impressions as equal to God's written Word.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Why is Scripture the essential standard for recognizing truth and spiritual guidance?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Holy Spirit, open my understanding as I read Scripture and direct my attention to Christ.
lessons.practicalStep: Before your next Bible reading, pray for understanding; afterward, write the passage’s main truth in one sentence.

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit Produces Spiritual Fruit

keyVerse.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,

lessons.devotionalThought: The Holy Spirit produces character that reflects Christ. Spiritual fruit is more than outward behavior; it grows as believers walk in dependence on the Spirit rather than yielding to sinful desires. This growth is often gradual, but it should be real. We cooperate by turning from sin, obeying Scripture, and relying on the Spirit instead of trying to transform ourselves through willpower alone.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which aspect of the Spirit’s fruit do you most need Him to develop in you?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Holy Spirit, help me turn from sinful desires and produce Christlike character in my life.
lessons.practicalStep: Choose one quality from Galatians 5:22–23 and identify one concrete way to practice it today.

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit Helps Us Pray

keyVerse.text: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.

lessons.devotionalThought: Believers do not always know how to pray, especially during suffering or confusion. The Holy Spirit helps in our weakness and intercedes according to God’s will. Praying in dependence on the Spirit does not require impressive language. It means coming to God through Christ, guided by Scripture, with humility and confidence that the Spirit is at work even when words are difficult.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How does the Spirit’s help encourage you when you do not know what to pray?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Holy Spirit, help me in my weakness and guide my prayers according to God’s will.
lessons.practicalStep: Bring one difficult concern to God honestly, then spend a quiet moment trusting the Spirit’s help.

lessons.title: Walk in Dependence on the Holy Spirit

keyVerse.text: This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.

lessons.devotionalThought: To walk in the Spirit is to live in continuing dependence on Him. Paul contrasts Spirit-filled living with being controlled by sinful desires. A Spirit-filled life is shaped by wisdom, worship, thanksgiving, humility, and obedience. This is not a one-time emotional experience but a daily surrender in which believers allow God’s Word to direct their choices and rely on the Spirit for strength. Every believer receives the Holy Spirit when they belong to Christ, but Scripture also calls Christians to continually be filled with the Spirit. This means living under His influence and direction, allowing Him to shape our attitudes, actions, worship, and relationships.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What area of your daily life most needs to come under the Spirit’s direction?
lessons.prayerPrompt: Holy Spirit, fill and guide me. Help me obey God’s Word and depend on Your strength today.
lessons.practicalStep: Begin today by surrendering your schedule, conversations, attitudes, and decisions to God, asking the Spirit to help you obey.

lessons.title: The Promise of the Spirit

keyVerse.text: And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that Jesus connects the coming of the Comforter with love, obedience, and His continuing presence with believers. The passage presents the Holy Spirit as God’s provision so that Christ’s followers are not left comfortless.

lessons.title: The Spirit Teaches Believers

keyVerse.text: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe that Jesus originally promised His apostles that the Holy Spirit would teach them and bring His words to their remembrance. This promise helps explain the trustworthy apostolic witness preserved in Scripture. Believers today depend upon the same Holy Spirit to illuminate God's written Word and help them understand and obey Christ's teaching; they should not assume the apostles' unique promise of remembrance applies to them in precisely the same way.

lessons.title: The Spirit Testifies of Christ

keyVerse.text: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that the Spirit’s testimony centers on Jesus and proceeds from the Father. The disciples are also called to bear witness because they had been with Christ from the beginning.

lessons.title: The Spirit Convicts the World

keyVerse.text: And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment:

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the three areas the Spirit brings to light: sin, righteousness, and judgment. Notice how Jesus explains each one in relation to unbelief, His return to the Father, and the judgment of the ruler of this world.

lessons.title: The Spirit Guides into Truth

keyVerse.text: Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth:

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that Jesus addressed the apostles when He promised that the Spirit of truth would guide them into all truth. This promise belongs first to their foundational witness to Christ and His teaching. Christians today rely on the Spirit's illumination as they read the authoritative Scriptures rather than claiming the same role of receiving foundational apostolic revelation. The Spirit's work continues to honor and glorify Jesus Christ.

lessons.title: The Spirit Gives Power

keyVerse.text: But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me

lessons.readingFocus: Observe that the promised power of the Holy Spirit equips believers to be witnesses for Christ. Notice the widening geographical movement from Jerusalem to the uttermost part of the earth.

lessons.title: The Spirit Dwells Within

keyVerse.text: But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the contrast between living in the flesh and belonging to Christ through the indwelling Spirit. The same Spirit who raised Jesus gives life to those in whom He dwells.

lessons.title: The Spirit Leads God’s Children

keyVerse.text: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how Paul identifies those led by the Spirit as God's children and describes their adoption, assurance, and inheritance in Christ. Being led by the Spirit in this context concerns the believer's new life and putting sinful deeds to death, not primarily receiving private directions about every personal decision. The Spirit enables Christians to live as those who belong to their heavenly Father.

lessons.title: The Fruit of the Spirit

keyVerse.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the contrast between the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit. The Spirit forms Christlike character in believers as they walk by Him. The fruit of the Spirit is not a promise of instant perfection but evidence of His continuing sanctifying work.

lessons.title: Walking in the Spirit

keyVerse.text: If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe that belonging to Christ includes a decisive break with the passions and desires of the flesh. Notice that life in the Spirit is meant to shape the believer’s daily walk and relationships.

lessons.title: Desire God’s Word

keyVerse.text: But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the contrast between the counsel of the ungodly and delight in God’s law. The fruitful tree illustrates the stability and spiritual nourishment associated with sustained meditation on Scripture.

lessons.title: Approach Scripture as God’s Word

keyVerse.text: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:

lessons.readingFocus: Observe what the passage says about Scripture’s divine origin and its usefulness. Notice the four ways it equips God’s servant for every good work.

lessons.title: Ask God for Understanding

keyVerse.text: Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the psalmist’s dependence on God for insight into His Word. Observe how wonder, longing, obedience, and counsel all shape the way he approaches Scripture.

lessons.title: Read Carefully

keyVerse.text: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the care taken to read the law clearly and explain its meaning. Notice the people’s attentiveness and the shared effort to help them understand what was read.

lessons.title: Study Diligently

keyVerse.text: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the Bereans’ readiness to receive teaching and their daily examination of Scripture. Their example joins openness to instruction with careful verification from God’s Word.

lessons.title: Read Scripture in Light of Christ

keyVerse.text: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how the risen Jesus explains the Scriptures as pointing to Himself and the fulfillment of God's saving plan. He begins with Moses and the prophets and later opens the disciples' understanding of the Law, Prophets, and Psalms. Careful Bible study considers a passage's original context while recognizing its place within the larger biblical story fulfilled in Christ.

lessons.title: Meditate on What You Read

keyVerse.text: This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night

lessons.readingFocus: God originally gave these instructions to Joshua as he prepared to lead Israel into the Promised Land. Notice the close connection between meditating upon God's law and obeying it faithfully. Christians can learn the value of sustained attention to Scripture without assuming that every promise associated with Joshua's specific leadership commission applies directly to them.

lessons.title: Receive the Word Humbly

keyVerse.text: Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the attitudes James says should accompany receiving the Word: humility, restraint, and openness to correction. Notice how the implanted Word is contrasted with the moral uncleanness that must be put away.

lessons.title: Obey What You Learn

keyVerse.text: But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice James’s contrast between merely hearing and actively doing the Word. The mirror illustration shows how quickly truth can be forgotten when it is not followed by obedience.

lessons.title: Handle Truth Faithfully

keyVerse.text: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice Paul's concern that God's Word be handled accurately rather than distorted through empty disputes and false teaching. Studying faithfully involves understanding Scripture in context, recognizing the author's intended meaning, and interpreting individual passages consistently with the Bible's wider teaching. Such care helps believers preserve gospel truth and avoid leading others astray.

plans.title: Growing in Your New Identity in Christ

lessons.title: A New Creature

keyVerse.text: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how Christ’s love, death, and resurrection reshape the believer’s identity and purpose. The passage connects new creation with reconciliation to God and a new way of viewing others.

lessons.title: A Child of God

keyVerse.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the contrast between the world’s rejection of Christ and the welcome given to those who receive Him. Notice that becoming God’s child rests on new birth from God, not natural descent or human effort.

lessons.title: Chosen and Accepted

keyVerse.text: According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that every spiritual blessing is found in Jesus Christ and flows from God's gracious purpose. Paul teaches that believers are chosen in Christ, adopted into God's family, and accepted through His grace. Our identity rests in what God has accomplished through Christ, and His purpose is that we grow in holiness and live for His glory.

lessons.title: Forgiven and Redeemed

keyVerse.text: In whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins:

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the movement from darkness into the kingdom of God’s dear Son. Notice how redemption and forgiveness are presented as present blessings believers possess in Christ.

lessons.title: Free from Condemnation

keyVerse.text: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the contrast between the law's inability through human weakness and what God accomplished through His Son. Those who belong to Christ are no longer under sin's condemnation. This freedom does not mean believers become sinless, but that their standing before God rests on Christ's saving work, and the Holy Spirit leads them into a new way of life.

lessons.title: Crucified with Christ

keyVerse.text: I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me:

lessons.readingFocus: Observe Paul’s repeated contrast between justification by faith in Christ and justification by works of the law. Notice how union with Christ’s death leads to a life now lived by faith in the Son of God.

lessons.title: Raised to New Life

keyVerse.text: For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how the believer’s life is described in relation to Christ’s resurrection, present reign, and future appearing. The passage directs attention from earthly priorities to realities above.

lessons.title: God’s Workmanship

keyVerse.text: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe that salvation is God’s gift and not the result of human works. Notice that good works follow salvation as part of God’s prepared purpose for those created anew in Christ.

lessons.title: A Chosen People

keyVerse.text: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people;

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that Peter describes believers collectively as God's chosen people, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation. These descriptions reveal their shared identity and calling in Christ. God has shown them mercy and called them out of darkness so that together they may proclaim His praises and live as faithful witnesses before the world.

lessons.title: Complete in Christ

keyVerse.text: And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power:

lessons.readingFocus: Observe Paul's call to continue walking in Christ, becoming rooted in His truth, strengthened in faith, and filled with thanksgiving. Believers are complete in Christ because everything necessary for salvation and reconciliation with God is found in Him. This does not mean spiritual growth is finished; rather, we continue growing from the secure foundation of our relationship with Jesus Christ.

lessons.title: God Is with You

keyVerse.text: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how God identifies Israel as His chosen servant and reminds His people of His covenant faithfulness. His promise of presence, strength, and help gave them reason not to fear. Christians today can draw encouragement from God's unchanging character and His faithfulness to those who belong to Him through Jesus Christ, without assuming that every specific promise to Israel applies directly to their personal circumstances.

lessons.title: Trust Instead of Fear

keyVerse.text: What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how David acknowledges both real fear and deliberate trust. Notice that confidence rests in God and His Word rather than in the absence of opposition.

lessons.title: The Lord Is Your Light

keyVerse.text: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the descriptions of the LORD as light, salvation, and strength. Observe how David’s confidence amid enemies is joined to his desire to dwell in God’s presence.

lessons.title: God Hears You

keyVerse.text: I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how David responds to God's deliverance with praise and invites others to join him in worship. His testimony reminds us that God hears His people and is worthy of our trust. Although Scripture does not promise that every danger or fearful circumstance will immediately disappear, believers can bring their fears honestly before the Lord and seek His help with confidence in His goodness.

lessons.title: Peace for a Troubled Heart

keyVerse.text: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the connection between the Spirit’s teaching ministry and the peace Jesus gives. Notice that Christ distinguishes His peace from what the world offers and addresses both trouble and fear.

lessons.title: A Sound Mind

keyVerse.text: For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how Paul encourages Timothy to remain faithful and courageous in his ministry rather than retreating in fear or shame. God's provision of power, love, and sound judgment equips His people for faithful service. This passage does not mean that experiencing fear or anxiety is automatically a spiritual failure. Instead, it encourages believers to depend upon God's strength and respond to difficulties with faith, love, and wisdom.

lessons.title: Give God Your Cares

keyVerse.text: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how humility under God’s hand is connected with casting cares upon Him. Notice the simultaneous calls to vigilance against the adversary and confidence in God’s restoring grace.

lessons.title: Pray instead of Worry

keyVerse.text: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how Paul directs believers to bring their concerns before God through prayer and thanksgiving. He promises that God's peace, which surpasses human understanding, will guard the hearts and minds of those who belong to Christ. This does not mean every anxious feeling or difficult circumstance will immediately disappear. Rather, believers are encouraged to continue bringing their concerns to God while trusting His faithful care.

lessons.title: God Is Your Refuge

keyVerse.text: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the repeated contrast between upheaval in creation and the secure presence of God. Notice how the refrain identifies the LORD of hosts as both present and protective.

lessons.title: Courage through God’s Presence

keyVerse.text: Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.

lessons.readingFocus: God spoke these words to Joshua as he prepared to lead Israel into the Promised Land. Joshua's courage was grounded in God's specific promise to be with him as he fulfilled that calling. Christians today can learn from Joshua's example of trusting God's faithfulness, obeying His Word, and acting courageously. Our confidence rests not in guaranteed earthly success, but in the faithful God who has promised to remain with His people through Jesus Christ.

plans.title: Learning to Hear God Through His Word

lessons.title: God Speaks through Scripture

keyVerse.text: All scripture is given by inspiration of God.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that Paul describes Scripture as breathed out by God and useful for forming a faithful life. Observe how teaching, reproof, correction, and instruction prepare God’s servant for every good work.

lessons.title: Listen with a Ready Heart

keyVerse.text: Speak; for thy servant heareth.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how the Lord called Samuel and how Eli helped him recognize that God was speaking. Samuel's experience was part of God's calling upon his life as a prophet. While Christians should not assume that God will speak to them in precisely the same way, we can learn from Samuel's humility, attentiveness, and willingness to obey. Today, we should approach God's written Word with that same receptive heart, seeking to understand and follow what He has revealed.

lessons.title: Receive the Word

keyVerse.text: Take heed therefore how ye hear.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how the different soils portray different responses to the same Word. Observe the qualities of the good ground: an honest and good heart, retention of the Word, and patient fruitfulness.

lessons.title: Recognize the Shepherd’s Voice

keyVerse.text: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how Jesus describes Himself as the Good Shepherd who knows His sheep, calls them, protects them, and gives His life for them. His sheep recognize His voice and follow Him because they belong to Him. This passage emphasizes the relationship between Christ and His people, not a requirement to hear an audible voice or receive personal revelations. Believers learn to recognize and follow Christ's teaching through Scripture, trusting the Shepherd who knows and faithfully cares for His own.

lessons.title: Let the Word Dwell in You

keyVerse.text: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how the word of Christ shapes teaching, worship, gratitude, and relationships within the church. Observe the virtues that surround this command, especially love, peace, forgiveness, and thankfulness.

lessons.title: Hide the Word in Your Heart

keyVerse.text: Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the verbs describing the psalmist’s engagement with God’s Word: seeking, hiding, declaring, rejoicing, meditating, and delighting. Notice how inward retention of Scripture is connected with purity and steadfastness.

lessons.title: Test What You Hear

keyVerse.text: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.

lessons.readingFocus: John warns believers not to accept every spiritual claim without examination. False prophets were spreading teachings that contradicted the truth about Jesus Christ. Notice how John directs believers to test these claims by their confession of Christ and their agreement with apostolic teaching. Christians today should evaluate spiritual messages, teachings, and personal impressions by God's written Word, rather than assuming that something is from God simply because it feels convincing or spiritually powerful.

lessons.title: Seek Wisdom from God

keyVerse.text: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God.

lessons.readingFocus: James encourages believers who are facing trials to ask God for wisdom, trusting His generous character. This wisdom helps us understand how to respond faithfully according to God's truth. Notice James's warning against being divided in our trust and commitment to God. Seeking wisdom does not guarantee that every decision or future outcome will become clear, but it teaches us to depend on the Lord and apply His Word with faith and perseverance.

lessons.title: Obey God’s Voice

keyVerse.text: Blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how Jesus redirects attention from physical relationship to faithful response to God’s Word. The brief exchange joins hearing with keeping rather than treating listening alone as sufficient.

lessons.title: Follow the Light of the Word

keyVerse.text: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how meditation on God’s law produces understanding and discernment. Notice the imagery of sweetness, restraint from evil, and light for the path.

lessons.title: Saved by Grace

keyVerse.text: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the movement from spiritual death to life with Christ. Observe that salvation originates in God’s mercy, love, and grace, excludes boasting, and results in a life shaped by the good works He prepared.

lessons.title: Grace through Jesus Christ

keyVerse.text: For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how Jesus Christ, the eternal Word made flesh, reveals God's glory, grace, and truth. God's grace was already evident throughout the Old Testament, but its fullness is revealed through Jesus Christ. Notice how John distinguishes the law given through Moses from the grace and truth revealed in Christ, through whom God's saving purposes find their fulfillment.

lessons.title: Justified Freely

keyVerse.text: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that God’s righteousness is received through faith in Jesus Christ apart from works of the law. Observe how grace, redemption, Christ’s blood, and God’s justice come together in the passage.

lessons.title: Confession and Cleansing

keyVerse.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice John's contrast between walking in God's light and continuing in darkness. Believers are called to acknowledge their sins honestly rather than deny or conceal them. Through Jesus Christ, we can confess our sins directly to God, trusting His faithfulness and justice to forgive and cleanse us. Confession does not earn salvation again; it is part of an ongoing relationship with God in which we acknowledge our failures and turn back toward obedience.

lessons.title: Sins Removed

keyVerse.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the descriptions of God’s mercy, patience, and compassion toward those who fear Him. Observe the images used to communicate the greatness of His mercy and the complete removal of transgressions.

lessons.title: Forgive as You Were Forgiven

keyVerse.text: Even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe the qualities believers are told to put on as God’s chosen people. Notice how forgiveness is patterned after Christ’s forgiveness and held together with love, peace, and unity.

lessons.title: Forgiveness from the Heart

keyVerse.text: So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the enormous difference between the mercy the servant received and the mercy he refused to extend. Jesus gives a serious warning against an unforgiving heart. We do not earn God's forgiveness by forgiving others; rather, those who have received His mercy are called to extend mercy themselves. Forgiveness does not mean excusing wrongdoing, removing necessary boundaries, or immediately restoring broken trust. It means turning away from personal vengeance and responding to others in a manner shaped by the grace we have received through Christ.

lessons.title: Grace Is Sufficient

keyVerse.text: My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice how Paul repeatedly asked the Lord to remove his thorn in the flesh, but the Lord answered by promising sufficient grace rather than removing the affliction. Christ's strength was revealed through Paul's continuing weakness. This reminds believers that God's grace does not guarantee freedom from every hardship or illness. Sometimes His sustaining power is demonstrated as we continue trusting Him through circumstances He has not removed.

lessons.title: Grace Teaches Holy Living

keyVerse.text: For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that grace not only brings salvation but also teaches believers how to live in the present age. Observe how Christ’s self-giving creates a redeemed people who are purified and zealous of good works.

lessons.title: Come Boldly to Grace

keyVerse.text: Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how Jesus is presented as the great High Priest who understands human weakness yet remains without sin. Notice that His priesthood is the basis for holding fast and approaching God’s throne with confidence.

lessons.title: Jesus Teaches Prayer

keyVerse.text: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice Jesus’ warnings against prayer performed for human attention or filled with empty repetition. Observe the order and priorities of the model prayer, beginning with God’s name, kingdom, and will before turning to daily needs and forgiveness.

lessons.title: Pray Continually

keyVerse.text: Pray without ceasing.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how continual prayer appears among a series of brief instructions concerning joy, thanksgiving, discernment, and holiness. Notice that the passage closes by emphasizing God’s faithfulness to sanctify His people.

lessons.title: Pray with Thanksgiving

keyVerse.text: In every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.

lessons.readingFocus: Notice that prayer and supplication are joined with thanksgiving rather than anxiety. Observe the resulting emphasis on God’s peace guarding the heart and mind, followed by instruction about what should occupy the mind.

lessons.title: Pray in Faith

keyVerse.text: Therefore I say unto you, What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them.

lessons.readingFocus: Observe how Jesus uses the withered fig tree to teach His disciples about faith in God and confident prayer. Genuine faith rests in God's power and faithfulness rather than our ability to produce a desired outcome. Scripture teaches that prayer must remain consistent with God's will and purposes. Notice also how Jesus connects prayer with a forgiving heart, reminding believers that trusting God should influence both their prayers and their relationships.

lessons.title: Pray according to God’s Will

keyVerse.text: If we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us:

lessons.readingFocus: Notice the confidence John gives believers who approach God through faith in Jesus Christ. Our assurance in prayer rests upon God's character and His willingness to hear requests that agree with His will.
